name: Glow-in-the-Dark PLA
chemical_makeup: PLA matrix loaded with phosphorescent mineral pigment, typically strontium-aluminate-based; the phosphor crystals are hard and angular, which is what makes this variant abrasive despite its modest filler fraction
summary: PLA carrying a strontium-aluminate phosphor that charges under light and glows in the dark. Printing temperatures are base-PLA-like (190-230 °C) and it has the best layer bonding of any filled variant in this cluster (Z 26 vs XY 32 MPa), but the phosphor is aggressively abrasive: a hardened nozzle is required, 0.2 mm nozzles are out, and it chews plastic AMS feeder components in a way base PLA never does.

printing.notes: Thermally this is base PLA — Bambu tests specimens at 220 °C and 200 mm/s and rates the material below 250 mm/s, so unlike pla-wood and heavy pla-metal there is no speed penalty. The delta is entirely abrasion: CNC Kitchen's nozzle-wear testing found glow filaments more damaging to brass than some fibre-reinforced materials (colorFabb GlowFill removed roughly 0.5 mm from a brass nozzle tip over a 100 g sample, while better-behaved brands such as dasFilament caused little wear). Use hardened steel and 0.4 mm or larger — Bambu explicitly advises against 0.2 mm nozzles because of phosphor particle size. Print thick: glow brightness and duration keep improving with wall thickness up to about 2 mm, with diminishing returns beyond.

feeding.notes: The sharpest feeding caveat in this cluster. Bambu's material table lists glow PLA as AMS-compatible but not recommended for AMS Lite, while forum users report the filament chewing through the AMS feeder inlet funnel within roughly 500 g and triggering motor-overload errors — abrasive wear on plastic feed components, not a jam. Experiences vary widely by brand and batch, matching CNC Kitchen's finding that abrasiveness is brand-dependent. Mitigations: feed from an external spool, fit an aftermarket metal/ceramic feeder-inlet protector, or use an AMS 2 Pro with ceramic inlet funnels. Rigid material, so drive system is unrestricted and no feeding assistant is needed.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping or steam at the nozzle and minimal stringing on a retraction test; extrudate should be smooth rather than pitted
drying.notes: Bambu specifies 55 °C for 8 h, matching base PLA. The mineral phosphor is not hygroscopic and no source reports an additive-driven moisture penalty — unlike pla-wood, where the filler absorbs water on its own.

storage.recommendations: Sealed bag or drybox with desiccant; same tolerance as base PLA. Light exposure during storage is harmless — it simply charges the phosphor

price.notes: Bambu PLA Glow around $24.99/kg, matching pla-gradient and pla-wood and above base PLA at $18-20/kg. Budget for nozzle wear on top of filament cost

recommended: thick-walled parts where glow duration matters (target 2 mm or more)
not_recommended: fine-detail prints needing a 0.2 mm nozzle
printing on a shared or expensive hotend without a hardened nozzle fitted
high-volume AMS-fed jobs without feeder protection
outdoor or hot-environment parts (base-PLA limits apply)

properties.notes: Bambu PLA Glow TDS: density 1.26 g/cm³ (only just above base PLA's 1.24, so the phosphor load is modest by mass), tensile XY 32±3 MPa and Z 26±3 MPa, elongation XY 8.6±1.2 % and Z 6.5±0.8 %, Tg 55 °C, HDT 55 °C at 0.45 MPa and 52 °C at 1.8 MPa. The Z/XY tensile ratio of about 0.81 is the second best in this cluster after pla-metal and far better than pla-wood's 0.58 — this variant's problem is hardware wear, not part strength. Thermal numbers sit slightly below base PLA.

compatibility.notes: Standard PLA-family bonding: welds to base PLA and other PLA grades, does not weld to PETG/ABS/ASA/PC/PA/PP. Practical workflow note — if you fit a hardened nozzle for glow, that nozzle stays in for the support material too, so plan a nozzle swap only if a finer nozzle is genuinely required for interface quality. Not recommended as a support material itself: it wastes an abrasive, expensive filament.

plate_recommendations.notes: Adheres normally at 35-45 °C with no release agent. Phosphor granules can read as slightly gritty on the plate-facing surface; smooth PEI gives a cleaner bottom face if that surface is visible.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Adheres normally; translucent glow bases carry the pattern well.

emissions.notes: No emissions delta from base PLA — the strontium-aluminate phosphor is an inert mineral at printing temperature and no unique fume hazard is reported. Standard good-practice ventilation for continuous printing still applies.

safety_notes: Not food-contact certified — the phosphor pigment is uncertified for that use. Fit a hardened nozzle before printing: brass wear from this material shows up as under-extrusion on subsequent, unrelated prints, so the cost of skipping it lands on the next job.
additional_notes: Glow performance is a design variable, not just a material one: charge under bright light (UV or daylight charges fastest) and build walls at least 1-2 mm thick, since brightness and afterglow duration scale with the amount of phosphor in the light path. Green-emitting phosphors are typically the brightest and longest-lasting; blue and other colours glow more dimly.

provenance.conflicts: AMS compatibility is directly disputed: Bambu's own material table lists glow PLA as AMS-compatible (excluding AMS Lite), while a long forum thread documents the material destroying AMS feeder inlet funnels within ~500 g and causing motor-overload errors. Recorded as 'conditional' with mitigations. Abrasiveness is strongly brand-dependent per CNC Kitchen — colorFabb GlowFill removed ~0.5 mm of a brass nozzle tip over 100 g while dasFilament caused minimal wear, so 'requires hardened nozzle' is set true for the category even though some spools would survive brass. Bambu's own wording is 'recommended for long-term printing' rather than required. UV stability of the phosphor pigment over long outdoor exposure is unverified.
